title: Vomiting blood in alcohol-related liver disease — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

blocks.text: Vomiting blood in alcohol-related liver disease — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

Round 5 • PACES Station 2: acute consultation • Skills C communication, E clinical judgement, F managing concerns, G welfare (with focused A/B/D where relevant) • 20 minutes • Educational examiner-style encounter • Prepared 14 October 2026 • Not an official PACES mark scheme
A 54-year-old with known alcohol-related cirrhosis presents after vomiting a large amount of red blood. They look pale and frightened. Assess, explain resuscitation and arrange definitive care.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Life-threatening upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage with suspected oesophageal or gastric varices. Trap: Do not wait for endoscopy to give terlipressin and antibiotics. Use individualised restrictive transfusion principles; avoid overtransfusion and assess aspiration risk.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Is this person unstable?
“First I need to check if this is affecting your immediate safety.”
ABCDE, observations and escalation.
Choose leading explanation
“I have a working diagnosis but need to exclude dangerous alternatives.”
Peptic ulcer bleeding, Mallory–Weiss tear and portal-hypertensive gastropathy remain possible until endoscopy.
Make treatment explicit
This is a serious bleed. We are treating the blood loss and starting treatment for possible swollen veins in the gullet before the urgent camera test.

Activate major haemorrhage/senior gastroenterology support, protect airway if active haematemesis or altered consciousness, 2 large-bore IV lines, group and crossmatch, FBC, clotting, renal tests. Give terlipressin and prophylactic IV antibiotics on suspicion, before endoscopy. Endoscopy after initial resuscitation with band ligation for oesophageal varices; consider TIPS if refractory.
Finish with prevention
I will ask if you want your partner updated. We will also address alcohol support and future prevention after the immediate danger is controlled.
Check patient priorities, understanding and follow-up.

blocks.text: Opening line: “There was a basinful of blood. Am I going to die? My partner is outside.” The actor is concerned but able to engage unless the examiner introduces deterioration. Release only history in the candidate brief; do not volunteer a diagnostic label. Ask “Why do you need to do that?” after proposed treatment. Acknowledge clear, compassionate explanations.

Q1. What is your immediate priority?
Model answer: ABCDE, protect airway as necessary, resuscitate with appropriate blood products and urgent senior/endoscopy support.

Q2. Are varices confirmed?
Model answer: No. Variceal haemorrhage is suspected because of cirrhosis, but peptic ulcer and other causes remain possible.

Q3. What treatment starts before endoscopy?
Model answer: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation when variceal bleeding is suspected, in addition to resuscitation. Continue terlipressin for up to 5 days (Baveno VII); prophylactic antibiotics, e.g. ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days.

Q4. When should endoscopy happen?
Model answer: After appropriate resuscitation, urgently; in severe unstable bleeding immediately after resuscitation, with timing guided by specialist local pathways.

Q5. What if oesophageal banding fails?
Model answer: Discuss urgent rescue options with expert hepatology/endoscopy/interventional radiology including TIPS.
Curveball: The patient deteriorates. Stop the routine consultation; summon emergency help and repeat ABCDE with immediate treatment.

FAIL — “Wait for endoscopy before starting treatment; we can discuss this when the tests return.” The candidate delays management of major haemorrhage.

PASS — “You have had a serious bleed and your blood pressure is low. We are treating this now, taking blood for crossmatch and urgently involving the bleeding and endoscopy teams. We will start medicines for suspected variceal bleeding before endoscopy.”

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — “We will resuscitate and monitor you while managing both a possible variceal bleed and other causes. We are starting terlipressin (for up to 5 days) and antibiotics such as ceftriaxone 1 g daily (for up to 7 days) promptly, and planning endoscopic haemostasis once you are sufficiently stabilised.”
